## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Large Language Models
  Code                    CSC_53432_EP
  Team and workload       Instructor: Guokan Shang (MBZUAI) · 24 h · 2 ECTS · theory + labs on LLM development and deployment: tokenization, architecture, pre-training and scaling laws, post-training (SFT, RLHF, DPO, GRPO), inference, RAG, agents, multimodality, evaluation and safety — and Shang's research.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (master's wiki)
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2} M2 program being finalized by the course instructors (the wiki indicates that the detailed M2 curriculum is still under development); course unit description confirmed by the wiki, SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who has already called a chat API or fine-tuned a small model and wants to know *why* the token cost explodes, why a RAG system hallucinates, or why DPO beats RLHF on a given budget.

**Empirical first**: we start from what goes wrong in practice — a perplexity that drops while the model stays useless, a KV-cache that runs out of GPU memory, a leaderboard score that does not survive production — and only then name the tools (tokenizer, scaling laws, alignment) that explain it.

The module covers the full LLM pipeline, from tokenization to safety, as theory and labs. It is a pillar of the M2: most other M2 modules build on it. The official volume is 24 h; these notes go deeper in places and flag what they add to the official description.

### What you will be able to do

-   Explain the complete pipeline for building an LLM, from tokenization to post-training.
-   Adapt a model cheaply — prompting and in-context learning, LoRA/QLoRA, distillation — and know when each is enough.
-   Implement alignment methods — SFT, RLHF, DPO, GRPO — and discuss their trade-offs.
-   Run an LLM in inference and master its costs and limits.
-   Build an in-depth RAG, beyond the basic tutorial.
-   Explore agents, multimodality and the perspectives they open.
-   Evaluate the performance and safety of an LLM with rigorous protocols.
-   Find your way in the literature and Shang's research work.

### Official objectives and syllabus

**Official description** (master's wiki): the SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet of this course unit is not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty); the description confirmed below is that of the wiki, which specifies the volume (24 h), credits (2 ECTS) and instructor.

An immersion into LLMs, mixing essential theory and hands-on work to develop both practical skills and conceptual understanding — with a view to the LLM development and deployment professions.

The syllabus starts with a brief panorama of historical NLP techniques, then addresses the transformer architecture (attention mechanism, tokenization) — the heart of modern LLMs —, the pre-training objectives (masked/denoising and causal language modeling, foundations of BERT, GPT and T5), the post-training techniques that refine a pre-trained model — instruction tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (PPO/DPO) and from verifiable rewards (GRPO) — and, finally, applications and future directions: RAG, agents, multimodality, alternative architectures.

The following table maps these official themes to the sections of the material.

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Post-training: instruction tuning (SFT)                                                     ch. 4 “Post-training: prompting, SFT and PEFT”
  RLHF (PPO/DPO) and verifiable rewards (GRPO)                                                ch. 5 “RLHF, DPO, GRPO”

Beyond this official description, the material adds three deepenings: inference in practice (ch. 6), LLM evaluation and safety (ch. 9) and the reading of Shang's research (ch. 10).

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module (period 1), 24 h for 2 ECTS, M2 badge. Three M1 courses prepare it: [Introduction to Text Mining and NLP](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html) for text processing, [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) for the transformer architecture, and [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) whose PPO sheds light on the RLHF and GRPO of the alignment chapter.

Downstream, it is the gateway to [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html), [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html), [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) and [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Background: from word2vec to transformers** — the trajectory leading from word embeddings to the architecture at the center of the module.
-   **Tokenization** — how text becomes a sequence of tokens, and why this choice matters so much.
-   **The architecture in depth** — the transformer dissected: attention, blocks, variants and implementation details.
-   **Pre-training** — objectives, data and costs of the model's founding stage.
-   **Post-training: prompting, SFT and PEFT** — going from the raw language model to the usable assistant: in-context learning first, then supervised fine-tuning, LoRA and distillation.
-   **RLHF, DPO, GRPO** — reinforcement learning methods and their alternatives for aligning models.
-   **Running an LLM: inference** — serving a model: constraints, optimizations and costs.
-   **RAG in depth** — plugging models into external knowledge, seriously.
-   **Agents, multimodality and perspectives** — LLMs that act, see and listen.
-   **Evaluation and safety of LLMs** — measuring what models really do, and containing their risks.
-   **Research (Shang)** — the papers of Guokan Shang, read with the module's grid (self-study).
-   **Exercises / Labs** — hands-on sessions that follow each stage of the pipeline.
-   **Projects and assessment** — solo and group project subjects, a written-exam proposal and a grading rubric.
-   **References** — the papers and sources of each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   Do the labs alongside the chapters: the LLM pipeline is understood hands-on.
-   Keep the full pipeline in mind — tokenization, pre-training, alignment, inference — and place each new development in it.
-   Review the M1 reinforcement learning module before the RLHF chapter: PPO is assumed known there.
-   Read the key papers as you go: each chapter has one or two that sum it up.
-   For each method, ask what it costs in compute and data: that is often what decides in practice.
-   Test evaluation concepts on your own model outputs: measuring is harder than it looks.

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} This module is the core of the LLM half of the master: the advanced LLM, safety, MLOps and speech modules of the M2 build on it, and the graph half joins it through GNN × LLM (Advanced GNN). Whether you aim at LLM engineering or a PhD, knowing *where* a model breaks (tokens, cache, evaluation) matters as much as knowing today's paper.
:::

## 0. Background: from word2vec to transformers {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1 modules)
:::

-   **Embeddings** (NLP ch. 4): word2vec/GloVe — a word = a *static* vector, derived skip-gram loss and negative sampling;
-   **Attention & transformers** (Deep Learning ch. 6): $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$, multi-head, residuals, LayerNorm; the "token graph" reading; BERT/GPT seen as applications (NLP ch. 7);
-   **Retrieval** (NLP ch. 2): TF-IDF and BM25 — the baselines of this module's retrieval (ch. 7); SBERT sentence embeddings (NLP ch. 7) for dense search;
-   **RL** (RL module): policies, policy gradients, PPO (ch. 5 of the RL module — the engine of alignment, ch. 5), bandits (ch. 4);
-   **Cross-entropy and perplexity** (ML ch. 3, NLP ch. 0): the pre-training loss is exactly maximum likelihood of the next token; $\mathrm{PPL}=\exp(\mathcal{L})$ in base e.
::::

This chapter places the module in its history: it recalls what M1 already established and the sequence of ideas that led to today's LLMs, so that each later chapter has a clear starting point.

**The trajectory**: n-grams → static embeddings → recurrent networks (LSTM) → attention (Bahdanau 2014) → transformer (Vaswani 2017) → BERT/GPT (2018-2019) → scaling (GPT-3, 2020) → alignment (InstructGPT 2022, RLHF) → general-purpose, multimodal, reasoning and agentic LLMs (2023-2026).

This module covers every technical stage of this stack, from the tokenizer (ch. 1) to safety (ch. 9), proving results that M1 left as claims.

::: note
[Module methodology]{.tag} Each chapter alternates *proved theory* (thm/prop boxes with proofs) and *labs* (nanoGPT, toy DPO, RAG, agent). The "NLP ch. N" references point to the M1 module Introduction to Text Mining and NLP, of which this course is the direct continuation: tokenization (NLP ch. 1 → ch. 1), BM25 (NLP ch. 2 → ch. 7), sentence embeddings (NLP ch. 7 → ch. 7), transformers (NLP ch. 7 → ch. 2).
:::

## 1. Tokenization {#ch1}

Before a model sees any text, a tokenizer cuts it into units from a fixed vocabulary; this chapter explains how that vocabulary is built and why the choice weighs on cost and quality.

A concrete scene: send the same prompt in French and in English to a Llama-style tokenizer. The French version typically costs 15–25% more tokens, so your context budget shrinks, and a rare word splits into six subwords — the model "understands" less and bills more.

This is why BPE, WordPiece and Unigram come *before* the architecture.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Mixing train/inference tokenizers; ignoring multilingual cost (latency + \$); treating UNK as a detail. All three sabotage a prod RAG as much as a nanoGPT lab.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Byte-level BPE: the exact construction]{.tag} BPE (proved step by step in NLP ch. 1) starts here from the alphabet of 256 *bytes*: any Unicode string can be represented without an "unknown" symbol. Learning loop:
$$\mathrm{merge}^{(k)} = \arg\max_{(a,b)}\; f(a,b),\qquad f(a,b)=\sum_{w}\mathrm{freq}(w)\,n_{(a,b)}(w),$$
where $n_{(a,b)}(w)$ counts the occurrences of the adjacent pair $(a,b)$ in word $w$ (counting weighted by word frequency). The merge is applied everywhere and one starts again until the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ reaches its target size $|\mathcal{V}|$ (32k-128k).

*Encoding* a new text replays the merges in the learned order (GPT-2/4, Llama). WordPiece (BERT) maximizes $\frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)f(y)}$; Unigram (T5) learns a generative model by EM then segments with Viterbi (NLP ch. 1.2).
:::

::: note
[Vocabulary, compression, multilingual costs]{.tag} The compression rate (characters/token) depends on the vocabulary *and* the language: vocabularies trained on English compress English well (\~4 characters/token) but degrade other languages.

Orders of magnitude measured in the lab: with GPT/Llama-type tokenizers, the same French text costs typically **15 to 25% more tokens** than in English; for poorly represented non-Latin scripts, the factor can reach **3× or more** (each rarely seen character decomposes into bytes).

Direct consequences: API cost (billed per token), context length consumed, and inequality of quality.

Llama 3 raised the vocabulary to 128k tokens — a large part of the gain serves non-English languages; GPT-4o (o200k) claims up to \~1.4× to \~4× fewer tokens depending on the language compared to the previous generation. Exercise 1 measures all this on your own texts.
:::

::: note
[Special tokens and security]{.tag} Special tokens (`<|endoftext|>`, `<|im_start|>`, template roles) delimit turns and documents. If the decoder accepts them in user input, an attacker can *inject* a fake dialogue turn or prematurely terminate a document (boundary confusion).

Defense: systematically re-encode input and neutralize special tokens (`encode_ordinary`, the `allowed_special` flag of `tiktoken`), never raw string concatenation around the prompt. This class of attacks returns in ch. 9 (prompt injections).
:::

```python
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o")
okapi = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-3.5-turbo")   # cl100k vocabulary

fr = "Les graphes pour les LLMs : une révolution pour la recherche d'information."
de = "Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän"
for s in (fr, de, "1234 + 5678 = ?"):
    print(len(okapi.encode(s)), "vs", len(enc.encode(s)), "->", s[:40])

# "safe" tokenization: special tokens are NOT decoded by default
b = enc.encode("end <|endoftext|> next", allowed_special=set())
print("ids :", b, "| decode round-trip ok :", enc.decode(b))
```

::: note
[Why it matters (M1 recall)]{.tag} Tokenization governs *cost* (length in tokens), *biases* (fuzzy arithmetic because "123 + 456" tokenizes poorly), *multilinguality* (the extra cost measured above) and real vulnerabilities (special tokens). Systematic diagnosis in the lab with `tiktoken` / `tokenizers`. For adapting an LLM to a low-resource language — vocabulary, template, data — ch. 10 presents Shang's work (Atlas-Chat, Nile-Chat).
:::

## 2. The architecture in depth {#ch2}

A language model must turn a sequence of token embeddings into a distribution over the next token, at a cost that stays manageable for long sequences. This chapter dissects the decoder-only transformer that does this in every modern LLM, and the design choices (normalization, positions, attention heads, experts) that make it trainable and cheap to run.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The decoder block]{.tag} An LLM stacks $n_{\text{layers}}$ blocks:
$$x \leftarrow x + \mathrm{MHA}(\mathrm{LN}(x)), \qquad x \leftarrow x + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(x)),$$
with **causal** attention (triangular mask: token $i$ sees only $j \leq i$), grouped heads (*grouped-query attention* for inference), a gated MLP (SwiGLU: three matrices with a hidden size of about $8d/3$, so that the MLP keeps about $8d^2$ parameters, as a plain 4× MLP would), **RoPE** positional embeddings (rotations; relative generalization to long contexts), and a final LN.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Pre-norm vs post-norm: the gradient flow]{.tag} **Post-LN** (original transformer): $x_{l+1}=\mathrm{LN}(x_l+F(x_l))$ — each block renormalizes *the residual itself*. The gradient of $x_L$ to $x_0$ crosses $L$ LN Jacobians whose product decays/explodes exponentially with $L$: warmup mandatory, fragile depth.

**Pre-LN** (GPT-2+, all modern LLMs): $x_{l+1}=x_l+F(\mathrm{LN}(x_l))$ — the residual path is *the identity*:
$$\frac{\partial x_L}{\partial x_l} = I + \sum_{l'\,>\,l}\frac{\partial F_{l'}}{\partial x_l}$$
→ a gradient that reaches every layer without multiplicative attenuation: stable training without fine warmup.

Price: the norm $\|x_l\|$ grows with depth (additive contributions), hence the **final LN**. (Xiong et al., ICML 2020.)
:::

:::: {#rope .thm}
[Theorem 2.3 — RoPE derived (Su et al., 2021)]{.tag} Position is injected by rotation: the dimension-$d$ vector is viewed as $d/2$ 2D pairs; pair $i$ of the token at position $m$ undergoes $R(m\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$:
$$R(\varphi)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}, \qquad q^{(i)}_m = R(m\theta_i)\,q^{(i)},\quad k^{(i)}_n = R(n\theta_i)\,k^{(i)}.$$

::: proof
**Relative property**: the dot product of a pair depends only on the *difference* of positions:
$$\langle q^{(i)}_m,k^{(i)}_n\rangle = q^{(i)\top} R(m\theta_i)^\top R(n\theta_i)\, k^{(i)} = q^{(i)\top} R\big((n-m)\theta_i\big)\,k^{(i)},$$
since 2D rotations commute and $R(a)^\top R(b)=R(b-a)$.

Summing over pairs = an attention score depending on $(n-m)$ and the contents — a "soft" generalization of relative embeddings.

Practical bonus: to extend the context, one *interpolates* the angles ($m\to m/L$) instead of relearning. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: {#kv-cache .prop}
[Proposition 2.4 — MQA/GQA: the memory arithmetic of the KV-cache]{.tag} The cache stores the keys and values of all past tokens. With $n_{\text{layers}}$ layers, $n_{\text{kv}}$ key/value heads of dimension $d_{\text{head}}$, $b$ bytes per element and $T$ cached tokens:
$$M_{\text{KV}} = 2\ (\text{K and V}) \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b \cdot T \ \text{bytes}.$$

**Multi-Query Attention** (Shazeer, 2019): a single shared KV head. **Grouped-Query** (Ainslie et al., 2023): $n_{\text{kv}} < n_{\text{heads}}$.

*Example* — Llama-3-8B: 32 heads, 8 KV heads, 32 layers, $d_{\text{head}}=128$, fp16:
$$2\times32\times8\times128\times2 = 128\,\text{KiB/token}.$$
A 100k-token context ≈ **12.2 GiB** (13.1 GB) of cache, versus about 49 GiB with full multi-head attention — a 4× reduction for nearly identical quality.

This is THE lever of long context (ch. 6).
:::

::: key
[Key result — KV-cache memory]{.tag}
$$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b \cdot T \ \text{bytes}$$
:::

::: {#moe .thm}
[Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): routing and balancing]{.tag} Each MLP block is replaced by $n_E$ experts $\mathrm{FFN}_1,\dots,\mathrm{FFN}_{n_E}$; a router $g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_g x)$ activates only the top-$k$:
$$y = \sum_{i\in \mathrm{top}\text{-}k} g_i(x)\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(x), \qquad \#\text{active params} \ll \#\text{total params}.$$
Capacity decorrelated from inference cost (Switch Transformer: Fedus et al. 2021; DeepSeek-V3: 671B total, \~37B active).

**Trap: routing collapse** — the winning experts attract everything. Auxiliary balancing loss (Switch):
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha_{\text{aux}}\, n_E \sum_{i=1}^{n_E} f_i\,P_i,$$
$f_i$ = fraction of the $k\cdot T$ routing slots of a batch of $T$ tokens sent to expert $i$, $P_i=\frac{1}{T}\sum_t g_i(x_t)$ = mean router probability.

Since $\sum_i f_i=\sum_i P_i=1$, balanced routing ($f_i=P_i=1/n_E$) gives
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}=\alpha_{\text{aux}},$$
the minimum over routings with $f_i=P_i$ (Ex. 9, by Cauchy–Schwarz). The loss never reaches zero, and the router's confidence plays no role: only the balance is rewarded.

Modern variants: fine experts + *shared* experts, balancing without an auxiliary loss (dynamically adjusted bias, DeepSeek-V3).
:::

::: note
[Efficient attention: FlashAttention and IO complexity]{.tag} Exact attention costs $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ compute but is *dominated in practice by input/output*: the naive implementation writes the $n\times n$ matrix to HBM (large, slow memory).

FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022): *exact* tiled computation that fits in SRAM, "online" softmax with an accumulator (running max $m$ and sum $\ell$ updated per tile):
$$m_{\text{new}}=\max(m,x), \qquad \ell_{\text{new}}=e^{m-m_{\text{new}}}\ell+e^{x-m_{\text{new}}}.$$
The $n^2$ matrix is never materialized; HBM reads are reduced from $\Theta(n^2)$ to $\Theta(n^2d^2/M)$ ($M$ = SRAM size).

The general lesson: *optimize memory access, not just FLOPs* (the GPU memory hierarchy, HBM versus SRAM, is in [Deep Learning ch. 6.3](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6)).
:::

::: def
[Beyond: SSM/Mamba (state equation sketch)]{.tag} A state-space model discretizes a linear system $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t),\ y=Cx$:
$$x_k = \bar A x_{k-1} + \bar B u_k,\qquad y_k = C x_k,\qquad \bar A = e^{\Delta A},\ \bar B \approx \Delta B,$$
computable in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ by a scan (no $n^2$ matrix).

The *selectivity* of Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023): $\bar B, C, \Delta$ depend on the input → content-dependent (selective forgetting), which yields attention quality at linear cost.

SSD duality (Mamba-2, 2024): the same computation rewrites as
$$y_k=\sum_{s\le k} C_k^\top\big(\prod_{s<k'}\bar A\big)\bar B_s\,u_s$$
— an "attention" with a causal kernel; hence the attention+SSM hybrid architectures. Continued in ch. 8.
:::

-   **Parameters: where are they?** embedding ($|\mathcal{V}| \times d$), attention ($4d^2$/block), MLP ($8d^2$/block: two matrices with a 4× expansion, or three SwiGLU matrices with hidden size $\approx 8d/3$; Llama 3 widens it to $3.5d$, about $10.5d^2$) — the rule
    $$\#\text{params} \approx 12\, n_{\text{layers}}\, d^2$$
    and the training memory cost (parameters + Adam + activations + gradients: \~20 bytes/parameter in mixed precision; cf. ch. 3 for actual compute);
-   **LLGA bridge**: attention *is* message passing on a token graph (Graph ML module ch. 5, Advanced GNN); graph transformers inherit from it.

## 3. Pre-training {#ch3}

Pre-training gives the model its knowledge of language by training it on trillions of tokens of raw text. This chapter answers three questions: which objective to optimize, which data to feed, and how to split a fixed compute budget between model size and data size.

::: thm
[Pre-training objectives]{.tag}

-   **Causal modeling (CLM)** — GPT: $$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$$ — predict the next token; generative by construction;
-   **Masked modeling / denoising (MLM)** — BERT (NLP ch. 7): mask \~15% and predict (bidirectional); excellent for encoding (classification, retrieval), does not generate;
-   **Span corruption / text-to-text** — T5: mask spans and regenerate them; everything is formulated as sequence→sequence.
:::

### 3.1. The data pipeline: quality, filtering, deduplication

-   **Curation**: web → rule-based filtering (length, code/punctuation ratio, languages), then *model-based* filtering (quality classifiers trained on reference pages — e.g. distilled judges); controlled mixture (web, code, books, articles, mathematics, synthetic data generated then filtered);
-   **MinHash-LSH deduplication** (proved in NLP ch. 8.3): k-gram shingles → MinHash signatures (a min-hash collision has probability equal to the Jaccard similarity) → LSH bands/ranks with
    $$\mathbb{P}_{\text{detect}}(J)=1-(1-J^r)^b$$
    → remove near-duplicates down to a threshold. At scale: tens of TB of text, approximately linear clustering; measured effect: less memorization, better benchmark (*deduplicating is regularizing* — LLMs learn duplicates "twice");
-   **Mixtures and curriculum**: per-domain proportions (annealing: raise quality/lower web at the end of training); *easy→hard* ordering (by perplexity) improves compute efficiency — demonstrated at scale by Shang (ch. 10, "Beyond Random Sampling");
-   **Multilingual**: balancing per language (otherwise the tokenizer and the model drift toward English — cf. ch. 1 and 10).

### 3.2. Scaling laws: decomposition and the Chinchilla optimum

::: thm
[Combined law (Hoffmann et al. 2022, "Chinchilla")]{.tag} The loss of a model with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens follows, over decades of scale:
$$L(N,D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},$$
$E$ = irreducible entropy of natural text; the other two terms = under-capacity and exhausted data (fitted on \~400 training runs; Kaplan et al. 2020 for the $L(N)$-only version). Reading: one must grow *N and D together*.
:::

:::: {#chinchilla .thm}
[Theorem 3.1 — The compute optimum, derived]{.tag} At fixed budget $C$, with $\mathrm{FLOPs}(C) \approx 6ND$ (2 per parameter × forward + backward, × D tokens):
$$(N^\star, D^\star) = \arg\min_{N,D}\; L(N,D)\quad \text{s.t.}\quad 6ND = C.$$

::: proof
Lagrangian:
$$\mathcal{J}=E+AN^{-\alpha}+BD^{-\beta}-\lambda(6ND-C).$$
Stationarity:
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{J}}{\partial N}= -\alpha A N^{-\alpha-1}-6\lambda D=0, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{J}}{\partial D}= -\beta B D^{-\beta-1}-6\lambda N=0.$$
Dividing side by side, $\lambda$ cancels:
$$\frac{\alpha A\,N^{-\alpha-1}}{\beta B\,D^{-\beta-1}} = \frac{D}{N} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\,D^{\beta} = N^{\alpha} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{N^{\alpha}}{D^{\beta}} = \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}.$$

The condition together with $6ND=C$ gives
$$N^\star\propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}, \qquad D^\star\propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)},$$
that is $N^\star\propto C^{0.46}$ and $D^\star\propto C^{0.54}$ with the fitted exponents ($\alpha\approx0.34$, $\beta\approx0.28$): *both grow roughly like $\sqrt{C}$*.

The ratio $D^\star/N^\star$ grows like $C^{(\alpha-\beta)/(\alpha+\beta)}\approx C^{0.1}$, so it is not a universal constant, and its value is very sensitive to the fitted constants.

Plugged into this formula, the published parametric fit of Hoffmann et al. (the exponents above, $A\approx406$, $B\approx411$) gives about 50 tokens per parameter at $10^{21}$ FLOPs and about 90 at Chinchilla's budget.

The rule $D^\star\approx 20\,N^\star$ comes from their two other estimation methods (fixed model sizes and IsoFLOP profiles), and a refit of the parametric law on their data (Besiroglu et al., 2024) recovers about 20 over the budgets of interest.

Either way, GPT-3 (300B tokens for 175B params, ratio 1.7) was "undertrained" at its budget. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the Chinchilla optimum]{.tag}
$$6ND = C, \qquad D^\star \approx 20\,N^\star$$
:::

::: note
[Compute and real costs (Llama 3, 2024)]{.tag} Orders of magnitude from the Llama 3 technical report (H100 training): 8B / 15T tokens ≈ 1.5M GPU-hours; 70B ≈ 7M; 405B / 15.6T tokens ≈ 30.8M GPU-hours (≈ 3,500 GPU-years, about 4 months on 10⁴ H100s).

At \~2-3 \$/GPU-hour, the 405B costs \~60-90M\$ of compute. This is why one "continues" from checkpoints rather than retraining ([ch. 4.3](#peft): LoRA, distillation).

It is also why the post-Chinchilla ratio went up: since inference costs daily, one deliberately *overtrains* small models (Llama-3-8B: 15T tokens ≈ 1900 tokens per parameter, \~100× Chinchilla) — the optimum depends on what is being optimized: the *training cost* (Chinchilla) or the *total cost* including inference.
:::

::: ex
[Lab: training a mini-GPT]{.tag} On a Shakespeare-type corpus (\~1 MB), train a \~10M-parameter transformer (nanoGPT): 30 minutes of GPU suffice to generate credible text. Observe: the loss curve, the effect of context, the sampling temperature (ch. 6). Extend: do exercise 8 (check the law $L(N,D)$ by regression on the published points).
:::

## 4. Post-training: prompting, SFT and PEFT {#ch4}

A pre-trained model only continues text; it does not follow instructions or hold a conversation. This chapter goes from the cheapest way to adapt it to the most invasive one.

It starts with prompting, which changes no weight (4.0), then supervised fine-tuning (4.1) and the reason a preference stage is still needed (4.2, continued in chapter 5). It ends with LoRA, QLoRA and distillation, which make fine-tuning affordable (4.3).

### 4.0. Prompting and in-context learning {#icl}

Before changing any weight, one can change the input. A well-prompted model is the zero-cost baseline that every fine-tuning must beat.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Zero-shot, few-shot, in-context learning]{.tag} A *zero-shot* prompt states the task and the query $x$. A *$k$-shot* prompt prepends $k$ demonstrations:
$$\text{prompt}_k = (x_1, y_1, \dots, x_k, y_k, x), \qquad \hat y = \arg\max_y\, p_\theta(y \mid \text{prompt}_k).$$
The weights $\theta$ do not change: the model picks up the task from its context alone. This is *in-context learning* (ICL), observed at scale with GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020).
:::

-   **Order and format sensitivity**: with the same demonstrations, some orders give near state-of-the-art accuracy and others near chance (Lu et al., 2022). Models favour the most frequent and the last label of the prompt; *contextual calibration* rescales by the probabilities given to a content-free input such as "N/A" (Zhao et al., 2021).
-   **What the demonstrations teach**: the format, the label space and the input distribution matter more than whether the demonstration labels are correct (Min et al., 2022).
-   **Chain-of-thought** (Wei et al., 2022): demonstrations that show intermediate steps, or simply "Let's think step by step" (Kojima et al., 2022), raise accuracy on multi-step problems for large models. Sampling several chains and voting is *self-consistency* (RLVR box of ch. 5); training the model to produce good chains with verifiable rewards is GRPO (ch. 5).
-   **Practice**: a system prompt for role and constraints, delimiters around untrusted content (9.4), an explicit output format, 3–8 diverse demonstrations, and the protocol of 9.6 to choose between prompts (Ex. 4).

::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — ICL as implicit Bayesian inference (Xie et al., 2022)]{.tag} Suppose each pre-training document is generated by first drawing a latent concept $\vartheta$ (topic, format, task), then text from $p(\cdot\mid\vartheta)$. The ideal next-token predictor marginalizes over concepts:
$$p(y \mid \text{prompt}) = \int p(y \mid x, \vartheta)\; p(\vartheta \mid \text{prompt})\; d\vartheta .$$
Each demonstration multiplies the posterior by its likelihood $p(x_j, y_j\mid\vartheta)$. When the demonstrations share one concept $\vartheta^\star$, the posterior concentrates on it as $k$ grows, and the prediction tends to $p(y\mid x,\vartheta^\star)$.
:::

Reading: ICL *locates* a task already seen in pre-training rather than learning a new one — hence the weak effect of wrong labels, and the failures on tasks absent from pre-training.

### 4.1. Supervised fine-tuning {#sft}

::: def
[Step 1 — Supervised Fine-Tuning (instruction tuning)]{.tag} Fine-tune the base model on quality (instruction, response) pairs — a few tens/hundreds of thousands of examples suffice to turn an autocomplete into an assistant. Engineering details: loss mask (the loss is computed only on the response), chat templates, data "distilled" from a large model.
:::

::: def
[Templates and loss mask — the detail that matters]{.tag} The template serializes the turns: `<|system|>…<|user|>…<|assistant|>`. The loss masks the *prompt* tokens (system/user roles) and keeps only the *completion* — otherwise the model learns to *imitate the user* and prompt logging becomes noise:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = -\sum_{t\,\in\,\text{completion}} \log p_\theta(y_t\mid y_{<t}, x).$$
:::

```python
# SFT with loss masking (HF TRL pseudo-code)
from trl import SFTTrainer

def format(example):                    # chat template + masked labels
    prompt  = f"<|user|>\n{example['question']}\n<|assistant|>\n"
    completion = example["answer"]
    return {"prompt": prompt, "completion": completion}
# - the loss is computed ONLY on the completion tokens (TRL SFTTrainer
#   does the masking automatically; in raw PyTorch: labels = -100 on the prompt)

trainer = SFTTrainer(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B",
                     train_dataset=dataset.map(format), ...)
trainer.train()

# pitfalls seen in the lab: template != inference template -> performance drop;
# padding token confused with eos; overly long answers -> silent truncation
```

### 4.2. Why alignment beyond SFT

::: def
[Step 2 — Why alignment beyond SFT?]{.tag} SFT imitates demonstrations; it does not directly optimize "the best response" and does not learn to avoid harmful responses. The central idea of InstructGPT/ChatGPT: **learn a human reward**, then optimize the policy against that reward (RL) — this is where the M1 RL module becomes the M2's central tool.
:::

::: note
[Rejection sampling (best-of-n)]{.tag} An intermediate and indestructible step: generate $n$ responses, keep those that pass a filter (reward model, tests, heuristics), re-fine-tune on them — the Llama 2 recipe between RLHF rounds (Touvron et al., 2023). This is exactly "exploit the best of $n$", without policy gradients; the link with bandits (RL module ch. 4) is direct: each draw informs the policy for the next round.
:::

### 4.3. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning and distillation {#peft}

Full fine-tuning of an 8B model with Adam needs about 16–20 bytes per parameter (ch. 2), well over 100 GB. Two families avoid this cost: train a few new parameters on top of a frozen model (LoRA, QLoRA), or train a smaller model to imitate a large one (distillation).

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — LoRA (Hu et al., 2022)]{.tag} Freeze a pre-trained weight $W_0$ of shape $d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}$ and learn a low-rank update of rank $r \ll \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$:
$$h = W_0x + \frac{\alpha}{r}\,BAx, \qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r},\quad A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{in}}}.$$

-   **Initialization**: $A$ random (Gaussian), $B=0$, so $\Delta W = BA = 0$ at step 0: training starts exactly from the pre-trained model.
-   **Scale $\alpha/r$** (`lora_alpha` in the PEFT library): changing $r$ barely changes the size of the update, so the learning rate need not be retuned for each rank.
-   **Parameters**: $r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})$ per adapted matrix instead of $d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}$.
-   **Merging**: after training, $W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ costs nothing extra at inference; or keep the adapters separate and serve many of them on one base model ([MLOps ch. 7](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch7)).
:::

*Example* — Llama-3-8B with $r=16$ on $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$ of its 32 layers ($W_K$ and $W_V$ map 4096 → 1024 dimensions under GQA):
$$32 \times 16 \times \big(2\cdot 8192 + 2\cdot 5120\big) \approx 13.6\text{M parameters} \approx 0.17\,\%\ \text{of the model}.$$

-   **QLoRA** (Dettmers et al., 2023): store the frozen base in 4 bits (NF4, a data type matched to normally distributed weights), quantize the quantization constants as well, and page the optimizer states to CPU memory on spikes. Gradients flow through the frozen 4-bit weights into bf16 adapters. An 8B base then takes about 5 GB, and a 65B model can be fine-tuned on one 48 GB GPU.
-   **Limits**: tasks far from pre-training (a new language, long continued pre-training) need a higher rank or full fine-tuning. LoRA learns less than full fine-tuning, but it also forgets less of what the base model knew (Biderman et al., 2024).

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Logit distillation (Hinton et al., 2015)]{.tag} A teacher with logits $z_t$ trains a student with logits $z_s$ at temperature $T$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = (1-\lambda)\,\mathrm{CE}(y, z_s) + \lambda\,T^2\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{softmax}(z_t/T)\,\big\|\,\mathrm{softmax}(z_s/T)\big).$$
A large $T$ exposes which wrong tokens the teacher finds almost right. The gradient of the KL term with respect to $z_s$ shrinks like $1/T^2$, hence the factor $T^2$, which keeps the two terms balanced when $T$ changes.
:::

-   **Token-level distillation** applies $\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}$ at every position of the sequence; teacher and student must share the tokenizer.
-   **Sequence-level distillation** (Kim & Rush, 2016) fine-tunes the student on texts generated by the teacher: this is the "data distilled from a large model" of 4.1, and the recipe of the small DeepSeek-R1 distilled models. It works across tokenizers.

## 5. RLHF, DPO, GRPO {#ch5}

This chapter continues chapter 4: once the model imitates good answers, we want it to prefer better answers to worse ones. It derives the three methods that do this — RLHF, which learns a reward and optimizes it with PPO; DPO, which skips the reward model; and GRPO, which uses verifiable rewards and no critic.

Notation: $\pi_\theta$ is the policy being trained, $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the frozen reference (the SFT model), $y_w \succ y_l$ a preferred and a dispreferred response to the same prompt $x$, and $\beta$ the KL coefficient.

::: thm
[RLHF — the classic pipeline (Ouyang et al., 2022)]{.tag}

1.  **Reward model**: train $r_\phi(x, y)$ on *human preferences* $y_w \succ y_l$ (response pairs); Bradley-Terry loss:
    $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{RM}} = -\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big).$$
2.  **Policy optimization** with PPO (RL module, ch. 5):
    $$\max_\theta\ \mathbb{E}\big[r_\phi(x, y)\big] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)$$
    — the KL term prevents *reward hacking* and out-of-distribution drift.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Bradley-Terry, derived]{.tag} If humans compare two responses $y_1, y_2$ with a probability of preferring $y_1$ increasing in the "strength" difference, the axiomatics (transitive binary choice, invariance) imposes a logistic model on the *difference* of latent scores:
$$\mathbb{P}(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)\big).$$
The log-likelihood of the observed preferences $y_w \succ y_l$ gives the loss above. Only the *difference* of rewards is identifiable: adding any function $f(x)$ to $r$ changes no preference probability.

This offset is harmless. In the KL-regularized objective it multiplies $e^{r/\beta}$ by a constant that the normalizer $Z(x)$ absorbs, so the optimal policy does not change (step 1 of Theorem 5.2). The KL penalty is there for another reason: to limit the drift away from $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and the over-optimization of an imperfect reward.

::: proof
Derivative in $r_w = r(x,y_w)$:
$$-\big(1-\sigma(r_w-r_l)\big)$$
— the penalty is maximal when the pair is misclassified, zero when the margin is amply positive; it is a logistic regression on reward differences. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[PPO for LLMs — a recall of the RL module]{.tag} The PPO-clip objective and the advantage estimates are those of [RL ch. 5](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch5), the prerequisite reading. For an LLM, the state is the prompt plus the tokens so far, an action is one token, the reward $r_\phi(x,y)$ arrives at the end of the sequence, and a per-token KL penalty toward $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is added along the way.

Four models in memory: policy $\pi_\theta$, reference $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (frozen), reward $r_\phi$ (frozen), critic (value head). Typical settings: $\beta\in[0.01,\,0.2]$, a learning rate about 10× below SFT, clip $\epsilon\approx0.2$.

Classic symptoms: KL explodes (β too small); degenerate responses (hacked reward); drifting length (verbosity bias of the reward model).
:::

:::: {#dpo .thm}
[Theorem 5.2 — DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): complete derivation]{.tag} The loss
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)$$
optimizes *the policy directly* on preferences — without a reward model or rollouts.

::: proof
**Step 1 (closed form of the KL-penalized problem: the Gibbs variational principle).** Fix $x$ and let $\pi^\star = \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\,e^{r/\beta}/Z$, with $Z=\sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y)\,e^{r(y)/\beta}$. For any policy $\pi$,
$$\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^\star) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[\log\frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} - \frac{r}{\beta} + \log Z\Big] = \mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) - \frac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbb{E}_\pi[r] + \log Z,$$
so
$$\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[r] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) = \beta\log Z - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^\star),$$
which is maximal exactly at $\pi=\pi^\star$:
$$\pi^\star(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\,e^{r(x,y)/\beta}.$$
This is the KL-regularised policy-improvement lemma of [RL ch. 6](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#kl-lemma), behind soft RL and SAC.

**Step 2 (implicit reward).** Inverting:
$$r(x,y) = \beta\log\frac{\pi^\star(y|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta\log Z(x).$$

**Step 3 (injection into Bradley-Terry).** In $\sigma(r_w-r_l)$, the term $\beta\log Z(x)$ — the same for $y_w$ and $y_l$ — *cancels*: only the difference of log-ratios matters.

Maximizing the likelihood of the preferences gives $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}$ above (with $\pi_\theta$ in place of $\pi^\star$).

**Gradient**:
$$-\beta\,\sigma(-\hat r)\,\nabla_\theta\big[\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)-\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x)\big]$$
with implicit reward margin
$$\hat r = \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w)} -\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l)}:$$
the log-ratio margin of the preferred responses is increased, all the more strongly as the pair is misclassified. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the DPO loss]{.tag}
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)$$
:::

The loss fits in a few lines of PyTorch. The only subtle part is the sequence log-probability: sum the token log-probabilities of the response only, with the prompt masked exactly as in SFT (4.1).

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def sequence_logprob(model, input_ids, attention_mask, labels):
    """log pi(y|x): sum of token log-probs over the response (labels = -100 on the prompt)."""
    logits = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask).logits[:, :-1]
    labels = labels[:, 1:]                                # token t is predicted at t-1
    mask = labels != -100
    logp = torch.log_softmax(logits.float(), dim=-1)
    tok = torch.gather(logp, 2, labels.clamp(min=0).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)
    return (tok * mask).sum(-1)                           # shape (batch,)

def dpo_loss(policy, ref, batch, beta=0.1):
    """batch["chosen"] / batch["rejected"]: (input_ids, attention_mask, labels) for y_w / y_l."""
    lp_w = sequence_logprob(policy, *batch["chosen"])
    lp_l = sequence_logprob(policy, *batch["rejected"])
    with torch.no_grad():                                 # pi_ref is frozen
        ref_w = sequence_logprob(ref, *batch["chosen"])
        ref_l = sequence_logprob(ref, *batch["rejected"])
    margin = beta * ((lp_w - ref_w) - (lp_l - ref_l))     # implicit reward margin r_hat
    loss = -F.logsigmoid(margin).mean()
    accuracy = (margin > 0).float().mean()                # share of pairs ranked correctly
    return loss, accuracy.detach(), margin.detach()

# sanity check: at step 0, policy == ref, so margin = 0 and loss = log 2 ≈ 0.693
```

:::: {#grpo .thm}
[Theorem 5.3 — GRPO (Shao et al., DeepSeekMath 2024): derivation]{.tag} For each prompt $x$, sample a *group* of $G$ responses $y_1,\dots,y_G$ from the current policy $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$ and score them. Every token of $y_i$ gets the same group-normalized advantage:
$$\hat A_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_{1..G})}{\mathrm{std}(r_{1..G})}.$$
With the per-token ratio
$$\rho_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})},$$
GRPO maximizes the PPO-clip objective with a KL penalty toward $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$:
$$\mathcal{J}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|}\Big(\min\big(\rho_{i,t}\hat A_i,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_i\big) - \beta\,\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{i,t}\Big)\Big].$$
The per-token KL estimator, evaluated at the sampled token,
$$\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{i,t} = \frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\pi_\theta} - \log\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\pi_\theta} - 1 \;\ge 0,$$
is unbiased for $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ under sampling from $\pi_\theta$, and never negative.

At the first update ($\theta=\theta_{\text{old}}$, so every $\rho_{i,t}=1$), the gradient of the clipped term is the policy gradient
$$\frac{1}{G}\sum_i \frac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})\,\hat A_i .$$

::: proof
**Variance.** REINFORCE, $\nabla\mathbb{E}[r]=\mathbb{E}[r\,\nabla\log\pi]$, stays unbiased with any *baseline* $b$ that does not depend on the sampled response:
$$\mathbb{E}[b\,\nabla\log\pi]=b\,\nabla\!\sum_y\pi(y)=0 .$$
The leave-one-out mean $b_i=\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}r_j$ is such a baseline (RLOO, Ahmadian et al., 2024), and the group mean is a rescaling of it:
$$r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_{1..G}) = \frac{G-1}{G}\,(r_i - b_i).$$
So the centred advantage is unbiased up to the factor $1-1/G$. It removes the variance due to the prompt's difficulty without training any network.

**The std normalization is a design choice, not a theorem.** Dividing by $\mathrm{std}(r_{1..G})$ gives every prompt the same weight, so an almost-solved prompt with a small spread is amplified: the gradient is biased toward such prompts. The $1/|y_i|$ factor also penalizes long wrong answers less per token. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) removes both; Ex. 11 measures the effect.

**No more critic.** Unlike PPO, the baseline comes from *the group itself* — the value network (and its memory and training) disappears. It is a Monte-Carlo estimate of the advantage $A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)$ obtained by sampling several responses. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[RLVR and reasoning (2024-2026)]{.tag} When quality is **verifiable** (a passing unit test, an exact mathematical answer), the reward no longer needs to be learned: *RL with Verifiable Rewards*.

GRPO is the engine of DeepSeek-R1: by optimizing verifiable correctness, *long chains of thought* emerge (self-verification, backtracking, "aha" moments) — the "o1" style.

**Self-consistency** at inference (Wang et al., 2023): sample $n$ reasonings and answer by *majority vote*. If the samples were independent and the correct answer had probability $p>1/2$ in a binary choice, the error of the vote would decay exponentially (Hoeffding):
$$\mathbb{P}(\text{majority wrong}) \le e^{-2n(p-1/2)^2}.$$
In practice the samples are correlated (same model, same prompt): the first few samples bring most of the gain, then accuracy saturates.

Costs: 10× more tokens; recent works regularize length (ch. 10: "Shorter but not Worse"). Exploration (bandits, RL module ch. 4) becomes central: the GRPO group *is* structured exploration.
:::

::: note
[Overview]{.tag} SFT (imitate) → RLHF (optimize preferences) → DPO (preferences without RL) → RLVR/GRPO (optimize verifiable truth). A "modern" LLM chains: base → SFT → rejection sampling → DPO/GRPO.

This is exactly the plan of the official course ("post-training methods"). In the lab: DPO on paper (exercise 10) then toy GRPO (exercise 11).
:::

## 6. Running an LLM: inference {#ch6}

A trained model still has to produce text, one token at a time, under memory and latency constraints. This chapter explains how tokens are chosen (decoding), where the memory goes (the KV-cache), and the three main ways to make serving faster or cheaper without changing the output much: speculative decoding, quantization and smarter batching.

### 6.1. Decoding: formulas and effects

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — From greedy to nucleus]{.tag} At each step, logits $z$ over the $|\mathcal{V}|$ tokens of the vocabulary;

-   **Temperature**:
    $$p_i = \dfrac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}$$
    — $T\to0$: argmax (greedy); large $T$: uniformization;
-   **Top-k**: truncate to the $k$ best logits then renormalize;
-   **Top-p (nucleus)**: smallest set of tokens with cumulative probability $\ge p$ (*adaptive* size: wide on an uncertain step, narrow on a deterministic step);
-   **Repetition penalty**: divide the logit of already emitted tokens (factor 1.1-1.3); **min-p**: threshold relative to the best token.
:::

  Setting                        Effect on quality                     Effect on diversity   Use
  ------------------------------ ------------------------------------- --------------------- -------------------------------
  T = 0 (greedy)                 deterministic, possible repetitions   none                  extraction, code, factual RAG
  Moderate T (0.7) + top-p 0.9   fluent, controlled                    moderate              general dialogue
  High T (1.0+), top-p 0.95      more hallucinations                   strong                brainstorming, synthetic data

### 6.2. KV-cache: the memory arithmetic

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Cache memory = $\mathcal{O}(n\cdot d)$, quantified]{.tag} In autoregression, each new token must attend to the keys/values of the whole past — they are cached, and their size $M_{\text{KV}}$ is given by [Proposition 2.4](#kv-cache), the formula to reuse.

**Llama-3-8B** (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim, fp16) → 128 KiB/token: 8k context ≈ 1 GiB, 100k ≈ 12.2 GiB (13.1 GB), 1M ≈ 122 GiB (weights excluded!).

Three ways out: GQA (÷4 here), int8 cache quantization (÷2), and eviction/recomputation (sliding window).

Engineering rule: *context length is first a memory bandwidth problem*, not a FLOPs problem — hence the techniques of the next sections.
:::

### 6.3. Speculative decoding: the correction proved

:::: {#speculative .thm}
[Theorem 6.3 — Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023)]{.tag} A small model $q$ proposes $\gamma$ tokens; the large model $p$ computes the $\gamma$ distributions *in a single forward*.

Each proposal $y$ is accepted with probability $\min(1, p(y)/q(y))$; at the first rejection, one resamples from the normalized residual $\mathrm{norm}\big(\max(0,\,p-q)\big)$.

Then the marginal distribution of each produced token is *exactly* $p$ — quality unchanged, latency divided by \~2-3 when $q\approx p$.

::: proof
For one token:

1.  acceptance contribution:
    $$q(y)\min(1,p(y)/q(y)) = \min(q(y),p(y));$$
2.  rejection contribution: the total rejected mass equals
    $$\sum_x q(x)\big(1-\min(1,p(x)/q(x))\big) = \sum_x \max(0,q(x)-p(x)) = R,$$
    and the resampled residual adds
    $$R\cdot\frac{\max(0,p(y)-q(y))}{R} = \max(0,p(y)-q(y)).$$

Total:
$$\min(q,p)+\max(0,p-q)=p.$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 6.4. Quantization: principles and errors

-   **Post-training int8**: nearly lossless (batch calibration, per-channel scales); **int4**: the standard compromise;
-   **GPTQ** (Frantar et al., 2022): layer by layer, minimize $\|Wx-\hat W x\|_2^2$ on a calibration set — column-by-column quantization *with error compensation* on the remaining columns (via the inverse of the Hessian $\mathbf{H}=2\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top$);
-   **AWQ** (Lin et al., 2023): protect the "salient" channels (high activations) with per-channel scaling *before* quantization — the error is shifted toward weakly active channels;
-   **Typical errors**: int8 ≈ +0.0-0.1 PPL; well-calibrated int4 ≈ +0.1-0.5 PPL (often imperceptible); below 4 bits, degradation accelerates (2-3-bit quantization = research); in production, always re-validate on *your* benchmarks, not PPL alone.

### 6.5. Serving: continuous batching, PagedAttention, costs

-   **Continuous batching** (vLLM, Orca): schedule at the *decoding step* — finished sequences leave, new ones enter the same batch; throughput multiplied by \~10-20× vs static batching;
-   **PagedAttention** (Kwon et al., 2023): the KV-cache split into pages (like virtual memory) — no more fragmentation; sharing of common prefixes (system prompt); \~2-4× memory gain → larger batches;
-   **Costs**: two regimes — API (on the order of \$/M tokens, steadily decreasing) vs on-prem (amortized GPU-hour: an H100 at \~3\$/h serving \~2-5k tokens/s on an int4-quantized 8B → a few \$/M tokens under heavy load).

    The real cost of an agent = repeated input tokens × history length (ch. 8); the "ML Ops" angle is deepened in the dedicated M2 module.

```python
# KV-cache arithmetic (prop. 2.4 / 6.2): Llama-3-8B
L, kv_heads, d_head, bytes = 32, 8, 128, 2
per_tok = 2 * L * kv_heads * d_head * bytes      # bytes / token
for ctx in (8_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    print(f"context {ctx//1000:4d}k -> {per_tok*ctx/2**30:6.1f} GiB of KV-cache")

# speculative ("assisted") decoding in HF transformers: small = proposes, large = verifies
# out = target.generate(**inputs, assistant_model=draft, do_sample=True)
# result: outputs IDENTICAL in distribution to the large model alone (thm 6.3)
```

## 7. RAG in depth {#ch7}

A model only knows what was in its training data, up to its cutoff date, and cannot cite sources. Retrieval-augmented generation fixes this by fetching relevant documents at query time and placing them in the context; this chapter goes through each stage of such a pipeline and how to evaluate it.

It assumes the minimal pipeline of [NLP ch. 7.4](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#minimal-rag) — chunk, embed, retrieve, prompt — and goes deeper at each stage.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)]{.tag}
$$p(y \mid q) \approx p_\theta\big(y \mid q, \mathrm{top}_k\, \mathrm{sim}(e_q, e_d)\big)$$
Index documents by embeddings, retrieve those closest to the prompt, inject them into the context.

Reduces hallucinations, updates knowledge, handles proprietary data *without retraining*.
:::

### 7.1. Chunking

-   **Fixed with overlap**: 256-1024 tokens, stride 10-20%; *structural* splitting (sections, paragraphs) > blind splitting (cut sentences destroy retrieval);
-   **Semantic chunking**: cut where the embedding similarity between successive windows drops (topic change);
-   **Multi-granularity**: index by passages, but return the parent section to the LLM (small-to-big); for structured documents, keep titles/metadata in the chunk (pre-retrieval filters).

### 7.2. Retrieval: BM25, dense, hybrid — with numbers

  Retriever           Principle                             BEIR (NDCG@10, \~18 tasks)   Strengths / weaknesses
  ------------------- ------------------------------------- ---------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------
  BM25                probabilistic weighting (NLP ch. 2)   ≈ 0.44 on average            zero training, exact (lexical matches); misses reformulations
  Dense (E5/BGE, …)   SBERT embeddings + ANN (FAISS/HNSW)   ≈ 0.50-0.52 for the best     captures paraphrase; errors on jargon/exact refs, must be indexed
  Hybrid + reranker   fusion (RRF) then cross-encoder       ≈ 0.53-0.55                  practical state of the art; reranking cost O(top-100)

::: note
[ANN indexes: IVF, HNSW, PQ]{.tag} Exact search costs $\mathcal{O}(nd)$ per query, and a million 768-dimensional float32 embeddings take 3 GB. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude in speed and memory (FAISS: Johnson et al., 2019).

-   **IVF** (inverted file): k-means splits the vectors into $n_{\text{list}}$ cells; a query visits only its $n_{\text{probe}}$ nearest cells, about a fraction $n_{\text{probe}}/n_{\text{list}}$ of the data.
-   **HNSW** (Malkov & Yashunin, 2018): a layered proximity graph; a query descends greedily from a sparse top layer to the dense bottom one in about $\log n$ hops. Fast and accurate, but memory-hungry: the links add roughly 100–300 bytes per vector, and the vectors stay uncompressed.
-   **PQ** (product quantization, Jégou et al., 2011): cut each vector into $m$ sub-vectors and replace each one by the index of one of 256 centroids, so a vector costs $m$ bytes — 96 MB instead of 3 GB above with $m=96$. Distances come from small lookup tables; IVF-PQ combines both ideas.

The figure of merit is **recall@k** — the share of the exact top-$k$ that the index returns — plotted against queries per second, and tuned by $n_{\text{probe}}$ (IVF) or the search width (HNSW). The table's NDCG figures assume a recall@k close to 1: measure it before blaming the embedding model.
:::

::: note
[Cross-encoder rerankers]{.tag} The bi-encoder scores $s(q,d)=\cos(e_q,e_d)$ *separately* (indexable); the cross-encoder scores $s(q,d)=f_\theta([q\,;d])$ *jointly* — it sees the exact term interaction (mini-attention) but must run on every candidate.

Hence the cascade architecture: dense/BM25 (top-100) → cross-encoder (top-5). Typical gain: +3 to +5 points of NDCG@10.

The "lost in the middle" effect (Liu et al., 2023): even with the right passages, the LLM exploits better those at the beginning/end of the context → reorder the best ones *at the extremes*.
:::

### 7.3. RAG evaluation

::: def
[RAGAS-type metrics (Es et al., 2023)]{.tag}

-   **Faithfulness**: decompose the answer into atomic claims (by an LLM judge); faithfulness = fraction *supported by the retrieved context*;
-   **Answer relevance**: the LLM generates candidate questions from the answer — average similarity with the true question;
-   **Context precision / recall**: are the useful chunks there and well ranked? / does the corpus contain what was missing?

Lab protocol: QA set with reference context (*golden context*), compare faithfulness with/without reranking, measure the cost (tokens, latency) of each stage.
:::

### 7.4. GraphRAG and variants {#graphrag}

-   **HyDE** (Gao et al., 2022): generate a *hypothetical answer* to the question and search *with its embedding* — the imaginary answer is closer to the documents than the question;
-   **Structured queries**: text → graph query (graph linearization, see the publications in ch. 10) or SQL (text-to-SQL): the LLM writes the query, the database answers — maximal auditability.

**Retrieval over a knowledge graph.** Vector RAG retrieves passages that *look like* the question; it fails when the answer needs a chain of relations, as in "drugs that target a gene associated with disease X". GraphRAG retrieves a *subgraph* of a knowledge graph of (head, relation, tail) triples, built as in [NLP ch. 6.4](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#relation-extraction) and [Graph ML ch. 10.1](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10).

1.  **Seed nodes**: link the question's entities to graph nodes, by string matching or dense retrieval over node descriptions.
2.  **Subgraph**:
    -   *k-hop*: every node within $k$ hops of the seeds — about $\bar d^{\,k}$ nodes per seed for an average degree $\bar d$, often too many beyond $k=2$.
    -   *PCST* (G-Retriever, He et al., 2024): nodes and edges get a prize that grows with their similarity to the question, edges a cost $c$; keep the connected subgraph $S$ that maximizes
        $$\sum_{v\in S}\mathrm{prize}(v)+\sum_{e\in S}\mathrm{prize}(e)-c\,|E(S)|,$$
        a prize-collecting Steiner tree with fast approximate solvers. The result is small, connected and relevant.
3.  **Linearization**: one triple per line, such as "(aspirin, treats, headache)", plus short node descriptions, with the instruction to cite node ids.

*Token cost.* Vector RAG sends about 5 × 300 = 1,500 tokens. At about 10 tokens per triple, the 2-hop neighbourhood of an entity of degree 30 (about 900 edges) costs about 9,000 tokens, and a PCST subgraph of 30 edges about 300: pruning keeps GraphRAG affordable.

*Global questions.* Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) also splits the graph into communities (Leiden algorithm) and has an LLM summarize each one, to answer questions about a whole corpus. The cost moves to indexing: one LLM call per chunk and per community.

*Benchmark.* STaRK (Wu et al., 2024) mixes textual and relational queries. Its STaRK-Prime split runs over the biomedical graph PrimeKG, with one text document per node, scored by Hit@1, Hit@5, Recall@20 and MRR; it is the benchmark of the final lab (ch. 8). The worked version, with a named corpus and baselines, is [Graph ML ch. 10.4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10).

```python
# minimal RAG (pseudocode with sentence-transformers + FAISS)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import faiss, numpy as np

enc = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
idx = faiss.IndexFlatIP(384); idx.add(enc.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True))

def answer(question, k=4):
    D, I = idx.search(enc.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True), k)
    context = "\n".join(chunks[i] for i in I[0])
    prompt = f"Answer using the following context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    return llm.chat(prompt)   # + citations = retrieved sources

# lab extension: cross-encoder reranking on the top-20, then
# RAGAS evaluation (faithfulness / answer relevance) on 30 questions.
```

## 8. Agents, multimodality and perspectives {#ch8}

So far the model only reads text and writes text. This chapter extends it in two directions: agents, which let it call tools and act in a loop, and multimodal models, which let images, audio and documents enter its context; it ends with the directions research is taking.

### 8.1. The ReAct loop, with a real trace {#react}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — LLM agent (ReAct, Yao et al., 2022)]{.tag} Perception-action loop (RL module ch. 7): **Thought** (reason) → **Action** (call a tool) → **Observation** (read the result) → iterate, until *Final Answer*. The LLM decides *when* and *how* to act; the tools bound its capabilities (exact computation, search, code).
:::

```python
Question: which M1 module covers HMMs?

Thought: I need to search the master's curriculum.
Action: search["M1 curriculum NLP HMM"]
Observation: ... CSC_52082_EP "Introduction to Text Mining and NLP",
             ch. 6 "Sequences: NER, HMM, CRF" ...
Thought: the answer is in the list of chapters.
Action: finish["The NLP module (CSC_52082_EP), chapter 6"]

# modern function calling: JSON typed by the chat engine
tools = [{"type": "function", "name": "search",
          "parameters": {"query": "str", "k": "int"}}]
# the model emits {"name": "search", "arguments": {"query": "...", "k": 5}}
# -> the runtime executes, reinjects the result, and the loop continues
```

::: note
[Planning and multi-agents]{.tag}

-   **Tree-of-Thoughts** (Yao et al., 2023): search a *tree* of reasoning steps, evaluate the nodes with the LLM, backtrack — beyond the linear chain (CoT);
-   **Multi-agents**: orchestrate a **DAG** of specialized agents (planner → retriever/coder → verifier → synthesis), LangGraph-type frameworks; each agent = an LLM with its own prompt/tools/memory; patterns: supervisor, debate, generator-critic.

    RL link ch. 7: policy decomposition; Graph ML link: *orchestration is an executed graph*;
-   **Memory**: scratchpad (the current context), *vector* memory (RAG over past exchanges), *episodic* memory (structured session summaries), external working memory (files) — it is the ch. 7 RAG reused on oneself.
:::

::: note
[Evaluating (and billing) an agent]{.tag} Benchmarks: GAIA (generalist assistant), SWE-bench (real GitHub tickets), WebArena and τ-bench (tools and dialogues).

-   **Task success**: the share of tasks whose *final state* passes an automatic check (the tests pass, the database holds the right record) — not a judge's opinion of the transcript.
-   **Reliability, pass^k** (Yao et al., 2024, τ-bench): the probability that $k$ independent runs of the same task *all* succeed. Run each task $n$ times, count $c$ successes, and average $\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ over the tasks.
-   **Cost per task**: tokens (often 10⁵-10⁶ for a multi-turn agent), tool calls and wall-clock time, divided by the success rate to get the cost per *solved* task — hence ch. 6: a small model for routine steps, a large one for decisions.
-   **Safety**: the rate of injections suffered (ch. 9.4).

With a per-task success probability $p$, pass^k equals $p^k$, whereas the code-generation metric pass@k (at least one success in $k$ tries) equals $1-(1-p)^k$. An agent with $p=0.8$ has pass@8 ≈ 1 but
$$\text{pass}^8 = 0.8^8 \approx 0.17:$$
a user who runs it every day has only a 21 % chance (0.8⁷) of a failure-free week (Ex. 14).

Agent evaluation is an open research topic — and a major career path of the master.
:::

### 8.2. Multimodality: how an image enters a context

-   **Vision**: a ViT encoder cuts the image into 16×16 patches → *one token per patch* ([Deep Learning ch. 6.6](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#vit) for ViT); a **projector** (MLP or Q-Former) aligns these tokens onto the LLM's embedding space → the image becomes "text" inside the context (LLaVA scheme).

    The encoder is often pre-trained contrastively image-text — the common latent space of CLIP, worked in [8.2b](#vlm) (and in depth in the Multimodal GenAI module ch. 5);
-   **Audio**: mel spectrograms → encoder (Whisper-style) → tokens; the "transcription + style" output feeds the LLM (voice assistant = encoder → LLM → synthesis pipeline);
-   **Video**: sampled images (1-4/s) + temporal pooling — very high token cost: the sampling step choice *is* a compression choice;
-   **Documents**: pages = images + interleaved OCR text (the number 1 enterprise use case — contracts, reports).

### 8.2b. Vision-language models, worked (self-study) {#vlm}

This self-study section (about 2 h, with Ex. 6) turns the vision bullet of 8.2 into a worked recipe: how an image becomes tokens, how CLIP aligns images and text, and how LLaVA plugs a vision encoder into an LLM. It is the vision-language recap that the Geometric Data module (ch. 8) points to.

-   **ViT recap** ([Deep Learning ch. 6.6](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#vit)): an $H\times W$ image is cut into $P\times P$ patches, each flattened and linearly projected, plus a position embedding; a transformer encoder processes the $HW/P^2$ patch tokens. ViT-L/14 at 336 px gives $(336/14)^2 = 576$ tokens.

::: def
[Definition 8.2 — CLIP's symmetric contrastive loss (Radford et al., 2021)]{.tag} Take a batch of $B$ image–caption pairs $(x_i, t_i)$, an image encoder $f$ and a text encoder $g$, with normalized embeddings
$$u_i = \frac{f(x_i)}{\|f(x_i)\|}, \qquad v_j = \frac{g(t_j)}{\|g(t_j)\|}.$$
With the similarities $s_{ij} = u_i^\top v_j$ and a learned temperature $\tau$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}} = -\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\Big[\log\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_{ij}/\tau}} + \log\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_{ji}/\tau}}\Big].$$
Each row (one image against all captions) and each column (one caption against all images) is a $B$-way classification whose correct class is the diagonal: InfoNCE in both directions. CLIP was trained this way on 400M web pairs.
:::

**Zero-shot classification** follows directly: embed one prompt per class, "a photo of a {class}", and predict the class whose text embedding is closest to the image embedding. No label of the target dataset is used.

-   **LLaVA** (Liu et al., 2023): a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 encodes the image; a projector $W$ (linear in LLaVA, a two-layer MLP in LLaVA-1.5) maps its patch features to the LLM's embedding space; the resulting visual tokens are placed in the prompt before the text tokens.
    -   *Stage 1, feature alignment*: freeze the vision encoder and the LLM and train only $W$ on about 600k image–caption pairs (filtered CC3M), the instruction being "describe the image".
    -   *Stage 2, visual instruction tuning*: keep the encoder frozen and train $W$ and the LLM on about 158k multimodal conversations, with the SFT loss mask of 4.1: the loss covers the assistant's answer only, never the image tokens or the user's question.
-   **Token budget**: 576 visual tokens for one 336-px image in LLaVA-1.5, as many as a page of text. High-resolution variants tile the image and multiply this count, which is why video (8.2) keeps few frames.

```python
# zero-shot CIFAR-10 with open_clip (Ex. 6) — pip install open_clip_torch torchvision
import torch, open_clip
from torchvision.datasets import CIFAR10

model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms(
    "ViT-B-32", pretrained="laion2b_s34b_b79k")
tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer("ViT-B-32")
model.eval()

data = CIFAR10(root="data", train=False, download=True, transform=preprocess)
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(data, batch_size=256)
prompts = [f"a photo of a {c}" for c in data.classes]

with torch.no_grad():
    v = model.encode_text(tokenizer(prompts))
    v = v / v.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)              # one text embedding per class
    correct = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        u = model.encode_image(x)
        u = u / u.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)          # image embeddings
        pred = (u @ v.T).argmax(dim=-1)               # nearest class prompt (cosine)
        correct += (pred == y).sum().item()
print(f"zero-shot accuracy: {correct / len(data):.3f}")
```


### 8.3. Perspectives

-   **Alternative architectures**: attention+SSM hybrids (ch. 2), xLSTM, latent transformers and diffusion language models (cf. ch. 10); the transformer does not have a monopoly;
-   **Small Language Models & distillation**: the quality/cost/latency trade-off governs enterprise deployment (distillation in [ch. 4.3](#peft), serving costs in ch. 6);
-   **Open research**: reasoning (ch. 5), long-term memory, LLMs *on graphs* (linearization vs structured embeddings — ch. 10 and the Graph ML/Advanced GNN modules), evaluation (ch. 9).

::: ex
[Final lab — vector RAG versus GraphRAG on STaRK-Prime]{.tag} The lab compares the two retrieval families of ch. 7 on one benchmark.

-   **Corpus and queries**: STaRK-Prime (Wu et al., 2024) — the PrimeKG knowledge graph with one text document per node; 200 queries drawn from the official validation split.
-   **System A, vector RAG** (7.2): BM25 + dense retrieval over the node documents, fused by RRF, top-20 reranked by a cross-encoder, top-5 in the prompt.
-   **System B, GraphRAG** (7.4): link the question's entities, retrieve a PCST subgraph (or a 2-hop one), linearize it with short node descriptions. The worked version is [Graph ML ch. 10.4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10).
-   **Metrics**: STaRK's Hit@1, Hit@5 and MRR for retrieval; RAGAS faithfulness and citation validity (does each cited node exist and support the claim?) for the answers; input tokens and latency per query.
-   **Deliverable**: a notebook and a one-page table split by query type (mostly textual, mostly relational), with paired bootstrap confidence intervals (9.6).

Extension: Ex. 16 adds an agent (8.1) that routes each question to System A, System B or both.
:::

## 9. Evaluation and safety of LLMs {#ch9}

A score on a benchmark is only useful if it measures what we think it measures, and a deployed model must resist misuse. This chapter covers how benchmarks are built and skewed, the biases of LLM judges, hallucinations, attacks on LLM systems, a statistical test to detect machine-generated text, and how to compare two models honestly; a self-study section on privacy and bias closes it.

### 9.1. Benchmarks: construction and contamination

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — MMLU-type benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2020)]{.tag} Multiple-choice questions (57 subjects for MMLU; variants: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HELM for multi-faceted evaluation). Two scoring modes: *log-likelihood* of the options (deterministic, but biased by answer length/frequency) vs *generation* then extraction (realistic, but prompt- and parsing-dependent).

Rule: always specify the protocol — rankings change with the mode.
:::

::: note
[Contamination: the measurement that skews everything]{.tag} If the benchmark is in the pre-training data (the web!), the score measures *memorization*, not competence.

Detection: n-gram overlap (8-13 grams) between questions/training data, canary strings (hidden markers), cloze recall tests.

Remedies: private/rotating evaluations, dynamic question generation, temporal re-splits (post-cutoff questions).

Recent work on this: memorization in fine-tuning and multilingual hallucinations — ch. 9 of the M1 NLP module (Buscaldi's work: MUCH, memorization prediction).
:::

### 9.2. LLM-as-judge: convenient, but biased {#llm-judges}

-   **Positional bias**: the judge prefers the first (or second) answer depending on order — mitigation: evaluate in both orders and average;
-   **Verbosity / style bias**: long, well-formatted answers are overrated — mitigation: rubrics (explicit criteria), constrained format;
-   **Self-preference**: a judge favors answers from its own model family — mitigation: judge ensembles, judges trained for calibration (references: MT-Bench, G-Eval);
-   **Calibration**: a judge score is not a probability — verify on a set where ground truth exists (fraction of judgments matching humans); cheap *distilled* metrics (FrugalScore, ch. 10) were born exactly from this need.

### 9.3. Hallucinations

::: def
[Taxonomy 9.2]{.tag} **Intrinsic**: the answer contradicts the source/context (RAG: wrong citation); **extrinsic**: unverifiable (invented) claims; **prompt fidelity**: silent disobedience to instructions.

Causes: sampling (temperature), knowledge cutoff, the "always answer" training bias (no learned abstention), sycophancy (telling the user yes).

Mitigations: RAG + verifiable citations (ch. 7), self-consistency (ch. 5), low temperature for factual tasks, abstention training, post-hoc verification by decomposition into claims (the heart of RAGAS "faithfulness").
:::

### 9.4. Attacks: jailbreaks and prompt injections {#attacks}

This section is the guaranteed source on jailbreaks and prompt injections for the modules that use them later — Control of Generative AI, Security and Robustness, MLOps and Advanced Topics in LLMs; the Explainability, Security and Privacy module (ch. 5–6) goes deeper.

-   **Direct jailbreaks**: role-play ("DAN"), hypothetical framing, encoding (base64, unicode), multi-turn crescendo — circumventing safety instructions;
-   **Indirect injections**: the *retrieved content* (web page, PDF, tool result) contains malicious instructions — the number 1 attack on RAG/agent systems (ch. 7-8);
-   **Defense in depth**: input/output classifiers (Llama Guard type), *spotlighting* (delimiting and marking untrusted content), least privilege on tools (the retriever does not write to the database!), prompt/data separation (ch. 1 — special tokens: the same hygiene), human in the loop for irreversible actions.

    No defense is complete — one *reduces* the attack surface.

### 9.5. Watermarking

:::: {#watermark .thm}
[Theorem 9.3 — Statistical watermark (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023)]{.tag} Before each token, hash the prefix → a pseudo-random seed that partitions the vocabulary into "green"/"red" (fraction $\gamma$, e.g. 1/2); generation penalizes reds. On a text of $T$ tokens containing $s_G$ green ones:
$$z = \frac{s_G - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\,\gamma(1-\gamma)}} \;\xrightarrow{T\ \text{large}}\; \mathcal{N}(0,1)\ \text{under H}_0 .$$
Reject "human text" if $z$ exceeds the threshold (p-value) — under H1 (marked), $z$ grows like $\sqrt T$ times the introduced bias.

::: proof
Under H₀ (unmarked text), each token is green with probability $\gamma$ independently, so
$$s_G\sim\mathrm{Bin}(T,\gamma);$$
the standardized variable tends to the normal (CLT), hence the z-score. The partition depends on the *prefix*: impossible to remove without the seed.

Limitations (follow-up paper, Kirchenbauer et al. 2023): paraphrasing, truncation, and false positives on short texts — the test is statistical, not deterministic. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 9.6. Comparing two models honestly {#compare-models}

A two-point gain on a 1,000-question benchmark may be noise. Before claiming that model B beats model A, measure the uncertainty due to the items, the prompt and the seed; this is the LLM form of [Machine Learning ch. 4.9](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#model-comparison).

-   **Pair the items.** Run A and B on the same $n$ items and record per-item outcomes $a_i, b_i$ (correct or not, or a score). Compute the standard error on the paired differences $b_i-a_i$: it is much smaller than the unpaired one when both models fail on the same hard items.
-   **Bootstrap over items.** Resample the $n$ items with replacement $10^4$ times, recompute the difference each time, and report the 2.5 % and 97.5 % percentiles as a 95 % confidence interval. This works for any metric: F1, judge win rate, RAGAS faithfulness.
-   **Paired test.** For right/wrong outcomes, McNemar's test uses only the discordant items: $n_{10}$ (A right, B wrong) and $n_{01}$ (A wrong, B right). Under H₀ (equal accuracy), each discordant item favours B with probability 1/2, and
    $$\chi^2 = \frac{(n_{01}-n_{10})^2}{n_{01}+n_{10}} \;\approx\; \chi^2_1 .$$
    For other metrics, a paired permutation test randomly swaps $a_i$ and $b_i$ within each pair.
-   **Worked example.** On 1,000 items, A scores 70.0 % and B 72.0 %, with $n_{01}=60$ and $n_{10}=40$:
    $$\chi^2 = \frac{(60-40)^2}{100} = 4.0, \qquad p\approx0.046$$
    (0.057 with the exact binomial version). An unpaired two-proportion test on the same accuracies gives $z\approx0.99$, $p\approx0.32$: ignoring the pairing hides a real, if small, difference.
-   **Prompts and seeds.** Scores move by several points with the prompt template and the sampling seed (4.0). Report the mean and the standard deviation over at least 3 templates and 3 seeds next to the item interval, fix the protocol (scoring mode, 9.1) before looking at the results, and correct for multiple comparisons (Holm) when many benchmarks are compared.

### 9.7. Privacy and bias of LLMs (self-study) {#privacy-bias}

An LLM can leak pieces of its training data and treat groups of people unequally. This self-study section (about 1.5 h) gives the core measurements; the Explainability, Security and Privacy module ([ch. 7–8](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html#ch7)) goes deeper.

::: def
[Definition 9.4 — Canary exposure (Carlini et al., 2019)]{.tag} Insert into the training data a *canary*: a template with a secret $r$ drawn uniformly from a space $\mathcal{R}$, such as "my PIN is $r$" with $|\mathcal{R}|=10^9$. After training, rank all candidate secrets by the model's perplexity on the template:
$$\mathrm{exposure}(r) = \log_2 |\mathcal{R}| - \log_2 \mathrm{rank}(r).$$
Near $\log_2|\mathcal{R}|$ (about 30 bits here), the secret can be extracted by sorting candidates; near 0, it is not memorized.
:::

-   **Extraction recipe** (Carlini et al., 2021): generate many samples from short prefixes; rank them by a memorization score, such as the ratio of the log-perplexity to the zlib entropy (compressed length in bits); check the top candidates against the training data. On GPT-2 this exposed hundreds of verbatim training sequences, including names, phone numbers and URLs.
-   **Membership inference as a test.** Decide H₀: $x$ was not in the training set, against H₁: it was. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma the best test thresholds a likelihood ratio; in practice the target's log-likelihood is calibrated by a reference model that did not see $x$:
    $$\Lambda(x) = \log p_\theta(x) - \log p_{\text{ref}}(x) \;>\; t .$$
    Report the true-positive rate at a low false-positive rate (0.1–1 %), not the AUC (Carlini et al., 2022). On large models pre-trained for about one epoch such attacks are close to chance (Duan et al., 2024); on small fine-tuning sets seen several times, they are not.
-   **Mitigations.** Deduplicate (3.1): a sequence present 10 times in the training set is generated about 1,000 times more often than one present once (Kandpal et al., 2022). Fine-tune with DP-SGD (clipping $C$, noise multiplier $\sigma$; ESP ch. 8), which suits LoRA because few parameters are trained (Yu et al., 2022). Remove personal data before training; never put secrets in a system prompt.
-   **Bias evaluation, BBQ-style** (Parrish et al., 2022): questions about two people from different social groups, in an *ambiguous* context (the correct answer is "unknown") and a *disambiguated* one. Among the answers other than "unknown", $n_{\text{biased}}$ follow the stereotype; the bias score
    $$s = 2\,\frac{n_{\text{biased}}}{n_{\text{non-unknown}}} - 1 \in [-1, 1]$$
    is multiplied by $(1-\text{accuracy})$ in ambiguous contexts. Report it per category (age, gender, nationality…) with a bootstrap interval (9.6).

## 10. Research (Shang) {#ch10}

Guokan Shang (lead research scientist, MBZUAI; PhD at the LIX laboratory, École Polytechnique, 2021, under the supervision of M.
