Vazirgiannis — the LLGA loop) works on the evaluation of generative models, efficient pre-training, multilingual LLMs and dialogue summarization. Three research axes are presented in detail, then the rest of his publications, each positioned relative to the chapters.

::: thm
[Axis 1 — Frugal evaluation: FrugalScore (ACL 2022)]{.tag} *Kamal Eddine, Shang, Tixier & Vazirgiannis, FrugalScore: Learning Cheaper, Lighter and Faster Evaluation Metrics for Automatic Text Generation* — [arXiv:2110.08559](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08559).

**Problem**: neural generation metrics (BERTScore, MoverScore…) cost one large-model forward *per pair* — prohibitive in a learning or LLM-judge evaluation loop.

**Method**: *distill* the reference metric (the scores, not the texts!) into a tiny student (T5-small), with an input representation compatible with the mother metric.

**Result**: correlation nearly preserved for a cost reduced by a factor of up to \~700× (plus pre-trained V2 variants).

**Position:** the "evaluation at an industrializable price" link of ch. 9 — evaluate often, at low cost, before evaluating well (heavy judges) on a subsample.
:::

::: thm
[Axis 2 — Curriculum in pre-training: Beyond Random Sampling (EACL 2026)]{.tag} *Zhang, Mohamed, Abdine, Shang & Vazirgiannis, Beyond Random Sampling: Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum Learning* — [arXiv:2506.11300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11300).

**Question**: does the order of pre-training data (ch. 3) matter, at constant compute?

**Method**: first systematic large-scale study (several hundred models of several sizes): curriculum by difficulty (perplexity, quality) easy→hard vs random mixtures.

**Result**: the curriculum improves the loss at fixed budget (better compute efficiency), with granularity choices that matter.

**Position:** the "curriculum & annealing" content of ch. 3 builds on this paper — an example of an engineering question (in what order to feed the model?) turned into measurable science.
:::

::: thm
[Axis 3 — LLMs for low-resource languages: Atlas-Chat & Nile-Chat (2024-2025)]{.tag} *Shang et al., Atlas-Chat: Adapting Large Language Models for Low-Resource Moroccan Arabic Dialect* — [arXiv:2409.17912](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17912) (1B/2B/3B models on 223B tokens of dialect; templates, SFT + DPO); *Nile-Chat: Egyptian Language Models for Arabic and Latin Scripts* — [arXiv:2507.04569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04569) (handling *arabizi* — Arabic in Latin script — at the tokenizer and pre-training level).

**Position:** ch. 1 (multilingual costs, vocabulary) and ch. 4 (SFT/DPO) applied to a real problem: adapting the LLM ecosystem to languages/scripts that dominant vocabularies penalize — the logical continuation of the extra-cost measurements done in the lab.
:::

::: note
[The other publications (with positioning)]{.tag}

-   **Meeting summarization** (the PhD thread): [unsupervised abstractive summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.05271) by multi-sentence compression + budgeted submodular maximization (ACL 2018 — the "graphical text mining" of M1 NLP ch. 8); [self-attentive abstractive communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09491) (AACL 2020); [speaker-change-aware CRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.02913) for dialogue acts (COLING 2020 — the CRFs of M1 NLP ch. 6); TACL 2023 survey ([arXiv:2208.04163](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04163)); French corpora [FREDSum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04843) (political debates) and [Claire](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16840) (spontaneous French dialogue); back to extraction: [discourse and extractive summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11055) (2024);
-   **LLM faithfulness and diversity**: "LLM as a Broken Telephone" (ACL 2025, [arXiv:2502.20258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20258)) — iterative generation distorts information (ch. 9); benchmark of [linguistic diversity of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10271) (TACL 2025); Markov generation chains (2026, [arXiv:2603.11228](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11228));
-   **Frugal RLVR**: "Shorter but not Worse" (2025, [arXiv:2511.01937](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01937)) — regularizing the length of math RLVR reasonings (ch. 5);
-   **Graphs & LLMs**: [graph linearization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19494) methods for reasoning with an LLM (ch. 7 — GraphRAG; bridge toward the Graph ML/Advanced GNN modules).
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **★ Multilingual tokenization.** Compare BPE vs Unigram vs SentencePiece on a multilingual corpus: compression (characters/token), coverage of numbers; measure the French "extra cost" over English for the same text.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): aligned professional translations (fr/en/de) → tokens/word; typically fr ≈ 1.15-1.25× en; German with compounds even more — until frequent compounds become tokens; check that o200k (GPT-4o) narrows the gap vs cl100k. Conclude on the real cost (context, API price) of the same application depending on the language. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **★ KV-cache arithmetic.** For Llama-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim) and a 128k-token context: compute the cache memory in fp16, then in int8, then with MQA; what maximum batch fits on an 80 GB GPU (int4 weights ≈ 5 GB)?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: 128 KiB/token (prop. 2.4) → 128k tokens = 16 GiB; int8 → 8 GiB; MQA (1 KV head) → 2 GiB in fp16, 1 GiB in int8. The available budget is ≈ 80 − 5 = 75 GiB, so the batch goes from \~4 sequences (GQA, fp16) to \~9 (GQA, int8), \~37 (MQA, fp16) and \~75 (MQA, int8): GQA/MQA and cache quantization *determine* the served throughput. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **★ Guided SFT with LoRA.** Fine-tune a small instructed model (1-3B) on 500 (question, answer) pairs from your domain with LoRA ($r=16$ on $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$): strict template, masked labels (code of ch. 4.1), 2-3 epochs. Count the trainable parameters; measure the effect of a wrong template at test time (a spectacular drop to witness once and for all).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: for Llama-3.2-1B ($d=2048$, 16 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 64, so $W_K$ and $W_V$ map 2048 → 512), Definition 4.3 gives
    $$16 \times 16 \times \big(2\cdot 4096 + 2\cdot 2560\big) \approx 3.4\text{M}$$
    trainable parameters, about 0.3 % of the model; the PEFT library's `print_trainable_parameters()` should agree. Track the loss on completion tokens only. With the inference template different from the training one, the answers lose the learned format and often continue the user's turn. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **★ Few-shot sensitivity.** On the SST-2 validation set (GLUE), with a 0.5-1.5B base model, measure the accuracy of $k$-shot prompting for $k\in\{0,1,4,8\}$, with 5 random orders of the demonstrations for each $k$. Then apply contextual calibration (4.0) and compare.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: score the two label words by their next-token probability rather than parsing free text. Expect the spread between orders to be large — several points, sometimes tens — and the predictions to lean toward one label. Calibration (divide the label probabilities by those obtained with the content-free input "N/A", then renormalize) usually raises the mean and shrinks the spread. Report mean ± range per $k$ (9.6). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **★ Watermark.** With $\gamma=0.5$ and $T=400$ tokens, compute $z$ for a text carrying 230 green tokens; threshold at 5% (one-sided); how many tokens are needed to detect a +5% green bias?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: $z=(230-200)/10 = 3$ → one-sided p ≈ 0.13 %: rejected (marked).

    For a green fraction $\gamma+\varepsilon$, the expectation of $z$ is $\varepsilon\sqrt{T/\gamma(1-\gamma)}$. It reaches the one-sided 5 % threshold 1.645 when
    $$T = \Big(\frac{1.645}{\varepsilon}\Big)^2\gamma(1-\gamma) \approx 271 \text{ tokens for } \varepsilon=0.05,$$
    which detects the bias only half the time. For 80 % power, replace 1.645 by $1.645+0.84$: $T\approx 620$ tokens — hence the difficulty on short texts. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **★ CLIP zero-shot and projector size** (self-study, 8.2b). (a) Count the parameters of LLaVA-1.5's projector, a two-layer MLP from the 1024-dimensional ViT-L/14 features to the 4096-dimensional embeddings of a 7B LLM (biases included), and compare with the LLM. (b) Run the open_clip code of 8.2b on CIFAR-10, then replace the single prompt by the average embedding of 5 templates ("a photo of a {}", "a blurry photo of a {}", …).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) the projector has
    $$1024\cdot4096 + 4096 + 4096\cdot4096 + 4096 = 20{,}979{,}712 \approx 21\text{M}$$
    parameters, about 0.3 % of the 7B LLM — stage 1 of LLaVA trains only these.

    **(b)** Expect roughly 90 % or more for ViT-B-32; the prompt ensemble typically adds about a point. Inspect the confusion matrix (cat/dog, automobile/truck). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
7.  **★★ RoPE.** Prove the relative property of thm 2.3 ($R(a)^\top R(b) = R(b-a)$), then check numerically that the attention score is invariant under a common translation of positions; implement context interpolation $m\to m/L$ and measure perplexity beyond the training length.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: 2D rotations = complex numbers — commutativity and $e^{-ia}e^{ib}=e^{i(b-a)}$; translation invariance follows from the theorem; in practice naive extrapolation degrades PPL, interpolation largely preserves it (this is the basis of extended contexts 32k→128k without full retraining). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
8.  **★★ Scaling.** From published data (LLaMA 1/2/3, Chinchilla), verify the law $\mathcal{L} \approx A N^{-\alpha} + B D^{-\beta} + E$ by regression; situate each model relative to the compute optimum (thm 3.1).
9.  **★★ MoE.** Derive the minimum of the auxiliary loss $\alpha_{\text{aux}} n_E\sum_i f_iP_i$ under the constraint $\sum_i f_i=1$ and show it corresponds to uniform routing; simulate the collapse (biased initialization of the router) without then with the loss.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: at router equilibrium, $P_i=f_i$; minimize $n_E\sum f_i^2$ under $\sum f_i=1$ → Lagrange (or Cauchy–Schwarz) → uniform $f_i=1/n_E$, where the loss equals $\alpha_{\text{aux}}$, not 0; without the loss, the winning expert attracts tokens (reinforced feedback) and specialization degenerates. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
10. **★★ DPO on paper.** Derive the closed form $\pi^\star$ of the KL-penalized problem (Gibbs variational principle), then the DPO loss by re-injecting into Bradley-Terry; check the gradient: it increases the log-ratio margin of the preferred responses $y_w$ over the dispreferred ones $y_l$. Then check numerically that the PyTorch loss of ch. 5 equals $\log 2$ when $\pi_\theta=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: follow the proof of thm 5.2 step by step — the key argument is that
    $$\mathcal{J}=-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}e^{r/\beta}/Z)+\beta\log Z;$$
    then $Z(x)$ disappears in the difference $r_w-r_l$.

    The gradient pushes $\log\pi(y_w)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w)$ up and the $y_l$ term down, modulated by $\sigma(-\hat r)$ (hard pairs first).

    At $\pi_\theta=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, $\hat r=0$ and the loss is $-\log\sigma(0)=\log 2$. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
11. **★★ Toy GRPO.** On a verifiable task (binary arithmetic), train a mini-model with GRPO (group of 8 responses); plot accuracy and response length — observe the emergence of longer "reasoning"; compare gradient variance with/without normalization by the group standard deviation, and with the leave-one-out baseline of thm 5.3.
12. **★★ Speculative, on paper.** Write out completely the proof of thm 6.3 in the case $\gamma=2$, then estimate the expected latency gain if $q=p$ on 80% of the mass but diverges on the rest.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: accept token 1 with probability $\alpha=\sum_y\min(q,p)\approx0.8$, then the second conditionally. With $\gamma$ draft tokens and i.i.d. acceptances, the expected number of tokens produced per target forward is (Leviathan et al., 2023)
    $$\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha} = \frac{1-0.8^3}{0.2} \approx 2.44 \quad (\gamma=2),$$
    at most $\gamma+1=3$; the limit $1/(1-\alpha)=5$ needs $\gamma\to\infty$. With a draft costing a fraction $c$ of a target forward, the speedup is $2.44/(1+\gamma c)$, about 2.2× for $c=0.05$. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
13. **★★ RAG vs context length.** Query an LLM with 4k/32k/128k of context over a corpus: does the "lost in the middle" effect appear? Compare with RAG; discuss the trade-offs (cost, faithfulness, indexing overhead).
14. **★★ Agent reliability.** An agent is run $n=10$ times on each task of a benchmark.
    -   **(a)** Show that $\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ is an unbiased estimator of $p^k$ for a task with success probability $p$ and $c$ successes.
    -   **(b)** For a task with $c=8$, compute the estimates of pass^1, pass^2, pass^3 and compare with the plug-in $\hat p^k$.
    -   **(c)** One run costs 60k input and 4k output tokens at 3 \$ and 15 \$ per million: what is the cost per solved task?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) $\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ is the average, over all $k$-subsets of the $n$ runs, of the product of their success indicators; each product has expectation $p^k$ by independence.

    **(b)** 0.8, $28/45\approx0.62$, $56/120\approx0.47$, against the plug-in 0.8, 0.64, 0.51, which is biased upward.

    **(c)** $0.18+0.06=0.24$ \$ per run, so $0.24/0.8=0.30$ \$ per solved task. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
15. **★★ Comparing two models.** On the 1,319 test problems of GSM8K, model A scores 61.0 % and model B 63.5 %, with $n_{01}=95$ problems solved by B only and $n_{10}=62$ by A only. (a) Run McNemar's test. (b) Compute a paired bootstrap 95 % interval for the difference from per-item outcomes you simulate with these counts. (c) Explain why an unpaired test is the wrong tool. (d) Say what you would add before publishing the comparison.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) $\chi^2=(95-62)^2/157\approx6.9$, $p\approx0.008$ (exact binomial: 0.0104): B is better at the 5 % level; at the 1 % level only the χ² approximation says so, and the exact test falls just short. (b) The difference is 2.5 points and the interval runs from about 0.7 to 4.3 points, excluding 0. (c) The unpaired test ignores that both models share the hard problems, which inflates the standard error. (d) Repeat over 3 prompt templates and 3 seeds, and fix the answer-extraction rule in advance (9.1, 9.6). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
16. **★★★ Agent project.** Extend the final lab of ch. 8 with an agent (8.1) that chooses, question by question, between vector retrieval, the graph retriever, or both.
    -   *Data*: STaRK-Prime, 500 queries of the validation split, plus 50 relational questions you write and check yourself.
    -   *Systems*: vector RAG, GraphRAG, the router, and an oracle that picks the better of the two retrievers for each query (an upper bound for the router).
    -   *Metrics*: Hit@5 and MRR; answer faithfulness and citation validity; tokens, latency and cost per query; the router's agreement with the oracle.
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository with a one-command evaluation, a 4-page report with per-query-type paired intervals (9.6), a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Rubric (20 points)*: reproducible baselines 5; router design and ablation 4; evaluation with paired intervals 5; cost analysis 3; error analysis of 20 failures 3.

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

**Official assessment: not displayed.** The master's wiki gives this course unit's volume (24 h), credits and instructor, but no assessment modality, and its SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet is not yet published. The proposals below are ours: a project (solo or in a group) plus a written exam, weighted as the instructor decides. They exercise O3 (large language models, the core of the course), O5 (graphs × LLMs), O7 (hands-on and industry practice) and O8 (trustworthy AI), and they prepare the Year-2 transverse project.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] The tokenizer tax: a multilingual and low-resource cost audit.** How much more does the same content cost in tokens across languages and scripts, and does extending the vocabulary pay off?
    -   *Implement*: characters per token and tokens per sentence for cl100k, o200k, the Llama-3 tokenizer and a SentencePiece Unigram model; then add 2,000–5,000 BPE merges learned on dialect text to a small open model, initialize each new embedding as the mean of its old sub-tokens, and fine-tune with LoRA (4.3), keeping the embedding and output rows trainable.
    -   *Data*: FLORES-200 (NLLB Team, 2022), aligned sentences in English, French, German, Moroccan Arabic (`ary_Arab`) and Egyptian Arabic (`arz_Arab`); the Moroccan Arabic Wikipedia dump for fine-tuning.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4-page report, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 1, 4.3, 10 (Atlas-Chat, Nile-Chat).
    -   *Success*: a cost table with bootstrap intervals (9.6), and a measured answer on whether the extension shortens dialect sequences without hurting English. Compare models in bits per character, not per-token perplexity, since the tokenizations differ.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Serving an 8B model on a budget.** What is the cheapest configuration that serves an 8B chat model at a target latency?
    -   *Implement*: serve Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with vLLM in AWQ and GPTQ int4 (fp16 if the GPU allows), with and without speculative decoding (draft: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, same tokenizer), at several batch sizes; measure throughput, P50/P95 latency and peak GPU memory.
    -   *Data*: 500 ShareGPT prompts, as in vLLM's benchmark scripts; the MT-Bench questions for a quality check. A 16 GB GPU (free Colab or Kaggle T4) suffices for the int4 runs.
    -   *Deliverables*: benchmark scripts, a 4-page report with a cost curve in \$ per million tokens, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 2 (Prop. 2.4), ch. 6.
    -   *Success*: measured KV-cache memory within 10 % of Proposition 2.4; the measured speculative speedup set against $\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$ with the measured acceptance rate; the int4 quality drop reported with an interval.
3.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Paper study: DPO versus PPO on controlled sentiment (Rafailov et al., 2023).** Does DPO reach a better reward–KL trade-off than PPO, as the IMDb experiment of the DPO paper reports?
    -   *Implement*: SFT of GPT-2 on IMDb reviews; preference pairs of sampled continuations ranked by a sentiment classifier; then DPO at four values of $\beta$, PPO (TRL) and best-of-$n$. Plot the reward against $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ on held-out prefixes.
    -   *Data*: IMDb (Maas et al., 2011); the reward classifier `siebert/sentiment-roberta-large-english` used in the paper.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4-page report stating which claims were and were not reproduced, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 4.1, 5.
    -   *Success*: reward–KL frontiers with 3 seeds per method, and a clear yes or no on the ordering of DPO and PPO at matched KL.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] From nanoGPT to an aligned assistant.** How far does each training stage move a small model, and at what cost in KL drift and response length?
    -   *Implement*: (A) pre-train nanoGPT models of three sizes and fit $L(N,D)$ against the compute optimum (3.2); (B) LoRA-SFT of Qwen2.5-0.5B on GSM8K solutions with masked labels, then DPO on pairs of correct and incorrect sampled solutions; (C) GRPO with an exact-answer reward, with and without std normalization and with the leave-one-out baseline (5.3).
    -   *Data*: TinyStories (Eldan & Li, 2023) for (A); GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) for (B) and (C).
    -   *Split*: one member per stage, one shared evaluation harness.
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository, a 6-page report, a 15-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 3, 4, 5, 9.6; PPO and REINFORCE from [Reinforcement Learning ch. 5](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch5).
    -   *Success*: scaling exponents with intervals; GSM8K test accuracy of SFT, DPO and GRPO compared by McNemar tests; KL and length curves.
2.  **[Group of 4 · ≈ 30 h each] GraphRAG versus vector RAG, with an agentic router.** For which questions does a knowledge graph beat a vector index, and can an agent tell them apart?
    -   *Implement*: Ex. 16 at full scale — hybrid retriever with reranking (7.2), PCST GraphRAG (7.4), ReAct router (8.1). The graph side follows [Graph ML ch. 10](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10).
    -   *Data*: STaRK-Prime (Wu et al., 2024), all validation queries; STaRK-MAG (academic papers) as a transfer test.
    -   *Split*: retrieval, graph, agent, and evaluation with the attacks — one member each.
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository with a one-command evaluation, a 6-page report, a live demo.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 7, 8, 9.2, 9.4, 9.6.
    -   *Success*: Hit@5 and MRR per query type with paired intervals; a router that beats the best single retriever and is compared with the oracle; citation validity ≥ 95 %; cost per 1,000 queries.
3.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 25 h each] Judging the judges, attacking the assistant.** How far can an LLM judge be trusted, and how easily is a RAG assistant hijacked?
    -   *Implement*: (A) position, verbosity and self-preference bias of two open judges against human votes (9.2); (B) an 8–13-gram contamination check of GSM8K and MMLU against a public pre-training corpus through the infini-gram API (Liu et al., 2024); (C) indirect prompt injections against a RAG agent before and after spotlighting and least-privilege tools (9.4), and watermark detection before and after paraphrase (9.5).
    -   *Data*: the MT-Bench human judgments (Zheng et al., 2023); BIPIA (Yi et al., 2023) for injections; the watermarking code of Kirchenbauer et al. (2023).
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository, a 6-page report, a 15-minute talk with a live attack.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 9; [Explainability, Security and Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) ch. 5–6 for the defences.
    -   *Success*: each judge bias measured with a paired test (9.6); attack success rates before and after each defence, with intervals; watermark z-scores before and after paraphrase.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

**Format**: 2 hours; one handwritten A4 sheet allowed; no electronic device; 4 questions — a course question, a computation, a short proof and a statistics question.

1.  **Question (5 points).** Compare RLHF (with PPO), DPO and GRPO: for each, say what is learned, what is sampled during training, which models sit in memory, and one typical failure.

    *Expected*:
    -   RLHF learns a reward model, then optimizes the policy online with PPO; four models (policy, frozen reference, reward model, critic); failures: reward hacking, length drift, KL explosion.
    -   DPO learns the policy directly from offline pairs, with no sampling; two models (policy, reference); failures: overfitting the preference set, likelihoods of both responses falling, no exploration.
    -   GRPO samples $G$ responses per prompt and uses a group baseline, with no critic; policy and reference plus a reward function; failures: prompt weighting biased by the std normalization, long wrong answers, the cost of $G$ samples.
2.  **Question (6 points).** A model has 40 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128, with a bf16 cache; its weights take 16 GiB of an 80 GiB GPU. (a) KV-cache bytes per token and per 32,768-token sequence (2 pts). (b) The largest number of such sequences served at once (1 pt). (c) With speculative decoding, $\gamma=4$ and acceptance rate $\alpha=0.7$, the expected number of tokens per target forward (1.5 pts). (d) LoRA with $r=8$ on $W_Q$ and $W_V$ of a 32-layer model with $d=4096$ and full multi-head attention: the trainable parameters (1.5 pts).

    *Expected*: (a) 2 · 40 · 8 · 128 · 2 = 163,840 bytes = 160 KiB per token, so 5 GiB per sequence. (b) (80 − 16)/5 = 12.8, so 12 sequences. (c) $(1-0.7^5)/0.3\approx2.77$ tokens, out of at most 5. (d) 32 × 2 × 8 × (4096 + 4096) = 4,194,304 ≈ 4.2M.
3.  **Question (5 points).** Let $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ be a reference policy, $r$ a reward and $\beta>0$.
    -   **(a)** Show that the objective
        $$\mathbb{E}_\pi[r]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$$
        is maximized by $\pi^\star\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\,e^{r/\beta}$ (3 pts).
    -   **(b)** Deduce that the Bradley–Terry likelihood of a preference $y_w\succ y_l$ does not involve the normalizer $Z(x)$, and state the DPO loss (2 pts).

    *Expected*: (a) expand $\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^\star)$ to get the identity of step 1 of Theorem 5.2:
    $$\mathbb{E}_\pi[r]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) = \beta\log Z-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi^\star);$$
    the KL is non-negative and zero only at $\pi=\pi^\star$.

    **(b)** Invert:
    $$r=\beta\log\frac{\pi^\star}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}+\beta\log Z(x);$$
    the term $\beta\log Z(x)$ cancels in $\sigma(r_w-r_l)$, and replacing $\pi^\star$ by $\pi_\theta$ gives the DPO loss (key result of ch. 5).
4.  **Question (4 points).** On 500 items, model A scores 80.0 % and model B 84.0 %; 15 items are solved by A only and 35 by B only. (a) Is B significantly better at the 1 % level (2 pts)? (b) A colleague runs an unpaired two-proportion test and finds $p\approx0.10$. Who is right, and why (2 pts)?

    *Expected*: (a) McNemar: $\chi^2=(35-15)^2/50=8.0$, $p\approx0.005<0.01$: yes. (b) The paired test: both models answer the same items, so the variance of the difference must be computed on paired outcomes. The unpaired test ignores that the models share their hard items, overestimates the standard error and loses power.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Question and baselines | 15 % | A precise question; strong, correctly configured baselines (hybrid retriever, SFT model, fp16 server) |
| Correct implementation | 25 % | Code that runs with one command; losses, masks and metrics checked on a toy case (the DPO loss equals log 2 at step 0) |
| Evaluation and statistics | 25 % | Paired intervals and tests (9.6), several seeds and prompts, a contamination check where relevant |
| Cost and systems analysis | 10 % | Tokens, latency, memory and \$ measured and compared with the formulas of ch. 2 and 6 |
| Safety, limits and ethics | 10 % | Failure cases, attacks or biases measured; limits stated honestly |
| Report and talk | 15 % | A clear 4–6-page report, figures with error bars, a 10–15-minute talk that answers the question |
